audience: HTTP/API engineers learning interview-sized CDN and HTTP caching reasoning for public and private responses. Focus on ordinary GET response caching; no prior CDN or HTTP cache knowledge is assumed.
prerequisites: An HTTP client sends a request with a method, URL, headers and optional body to a server and receives a response with a status, headers and optional body. GET requests retrieve a resource.
An API server can read and write a database; the database stores application data.

objectives.description: Define an HTTP cache, browser private cache, CDN shared edge cache, origin, cache hit and miss. Trace a GET for a public resource through the layers on a miss and on either kind of hit, including the returning response and storage subject to policy; distinguish cached HTTP responses from database records.

Define Cache-Control response directives, freshness and staleness. Explain max-age, shared-cache s-maxage precedence and Age; account for existing response age across layers rather than restarting freshness on delivery. Freshness permits reuse under policy and does not prove the origin has not changed.

Define representation, revalidation, ETag and If-None-Match. Trace an expired stored GET response through conditional validation: matching representation returns 304 without a replacement body and refreshes applicable metadata, while changed representation returns 200 with a new body and validator. Distinguish saved body bandwidth from avoided origin work.

Define cookies, Cookie/Set-Cookie, Authorization, authentication and authorization at a basic level. Distinguish unqualified no-cache, no-store and private response directives. Select explicit policies for public responses versus private responses. Explain that cookies, Set-Cookie and authentication are not automatic per-user cache keys or a universal CDN bypass guarantee; enforce authorization at the origin and verified shared-cache exclusion for private responses.

Define cache key, representation variant and Vary. Preserve URL/query and header distinctions that change response content; explain explicit CDN key configuration, Vary matching, wrong-content risks and reduced reuse from unnecessary fragmentation. Do not treat variant separation as permission to publicly cache private responses.

Choose versioned URLs for immutable public assets and a bounded freshness/revalidation policy for mutable published pages. Define CDN purge and explain its provider-specific reach, propagation and browser-cache limits. Distinguish a database update from cache invalidation and avoid promising instant revocation of already delivered content.

Define stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error as optional bounded stale-reuse permissions. Distinguish latency hiding from failure fallback, calculate bounds relative to freshness expiry, and require an existing eligible response and verified cache support/policy; do not promise universal availability or use stale public content where revocation or private-response correctness forbids it.

Define request hit ratio at a specified cache layer and estimate origin request load under explicit simplified assumptions. Explain latency, transfer and origin-load benefits versus CDN cost, operational complexity and cold or low-reuse traffic. Choose whether shared caching is worthwhile without exposing private content for a higher hit rate.

questions.question: A browser requests the public Notes logo with GET. Define HTTP cache, browser private cache, CDN shared edge, origin, hit and miss. Trace the request and returning response with empty caches, then a browser hit and a CDN hit from another browser. Explain what is stored and whether every request reaches the origin or database. Then consider this workload: In a simplified single-CDN setup, 1000 GET requests reach the CDN after browser caching; 800 are served without contacting origin and each remaining request makes exactly one origin request, with no background requests or extra layers. Define and calculate the CDN request hit ratio and origin request count. Explain why this does not measure browser hits, bytes saved or real total origin work. Compare repeated public assets with low-traffic mostly private Notes usage, including latency, bandwidth/load benefits, CDN charges and operational costs; when would you omit shared caching?
criteria: An HTTP cache stores reusable responses; a browser private cache serves one user agent, a CDN edge is an intermediary shared by users, and the origin is the server responsible for the resource.
On a miss the request travels browser to CDN to origin; the response returns origin to CDN to browser, with each cache storing only when its applicable policy permits.
A hit reuses a suitable stored response: a browser hit avoids the network request, while a CDN hit after a browser miss avoids the origin. A miss lacks a usable stored response.
These caches store HTTP response bodies and metadata, not database records; the origin may consult its database, but a hit need not reach that database.

At this layer, request hit ratio is requests served from CDN cache without contacting origin divided by requests reaching the CDN: 800/1000 = 80 percent. Under the stated assumptions the other 200 requests reach origin.

Browser hits never reached this denominator; request hit ratio is not byte hit ratio and differently sized responses change bandwidth savings. Real validation, refreshes, multiple layers and application work require their own measurements.
Nearby reusable responses can reduce user latency, origin requests and origin transfer, but CDN requests/transfer charges and configuration, invalidation and monitoring work add cost.

Repeated public assets and popular published pages can benefit; low traffic, low reuse or mostly private responses may not justify a CDN cache. Measure reuse, latency and total cost, and retain privacy rules rather than sharing private notes to improve hit rate.
criticalMisconceptions: Every cache hit still reaches the origin.
A CDN is a private per-user cache.
A CDN automatically replicates database records.
80 percent CDN request hits means 80 percent of all browser requests or bytes.
A high hit ratio proves the lowest total cost.
Every Notes deployment requires shared caching.

questions.question: A public published page has Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, s-maxage=300 and reaches a browser with Age: 90. Ignore transit and clock differences. Define these directives, freshness, staleness and Age; calculate whether the browser and CDN may treat this response as fresh, including each remaining lifetime. Explain whether delivery starts a new full lifetime or proves the origin page is unchanged. Later, The CDN has a stale published Notes page with ETag: "v1" and cannot serve it stale under its policy. Define representation, revalidation, ETag and If-None-Match. Trace the request to the origin and the response for an unchanged page and then a page updated to v2. State which body the CDN serves, what metadata changes, and whether validation avoids the network request or guarantees no origin/database work.
criteria: Cache-Control communicates response caching policy; public explicitly permits shared caching subject to applicable rules, max-age sets a freshness lifetime in seconds, and s-maxage overrides it for shared caches only.
A fresh stored response is young enough for reuse without validation under its policy; a stale response has exceeded that lifetime, which does not itself delete the stored body.
Age estimates seconds since origin generation or successful validation, including time through caches; delivery to another layer does not reset it.
At age 90, the browser lifetime of 60 has expired by 30 seconds; the shared CDN lifetime of 300 has 210 seconds remaining. Neither calculation says the origin has not changed.

A representation is the returned form of a resource; revalidation checks whether a stored representation remains usable; ETag is an opaque validator identifying it, and the conditional GET sends the stored tag in If-None-Match.

If the selected representation still matches v1, the origin returns 304 Not Modified without a replacement body; the CDN updates applicable stored metadata and reuses its existing body to serve the request.
If the representation has changed, the origin returns 200 with the new body and validator; the CDN replaces its stored representation if caching policy allows.
A 304 saves retransmitting the body across that validation hop, but the origin was contacted and might perform application or database work to decide whether it changed.
criticalMisconceptions: s-maxage overrides browser max-age.
Each cache starts a new full lifetime when receiving the response.
Fresh means guaranteed identical to the current origin.
304 contains the new page body.
Revalidation guarantees no origin request or database work.
An ETag forces immediate update of every cache.

questions.question: Notes serves public published pages and GET /api/notes for the signed-in user. Define cookies, Cookie/Set-Cookie, Authorization, authentication versus authorization, and response directives no-cache, no-store and private. Choose a policy for a public page that may be stored but must validate before reuse, a private note allowed only in the browser cache, and a sensitive note that must not be stored by HTTP caches. Explain why Cookie, Set-Cookie or authentication alone is not a universal per-user key or CDN-bypass guarantee, how shared reuse can leak data, and what authorization and CDN checks are required.
criteria: Cookies carry browser-held state: Set-Cookie asks the browser to store it and Cookie sends it back. Authorization is a request header carrying credentials; authentication establishes identity while authorization checks permission to access a resource.
Unqualified no-cache allows storage but requires successful validation before reuse; it fits a public page whose stored response must be checked each time.

Unqualified private forbids shared-cache storage while allowing a private cache to store subject to other directives; it fits a private note where browser storage is acceptable but does not itself require revalidation on every use.
no-store instructs HTTP caches not to store the response and fits the sensitive-note requirement; it is not an authorization check or a promise to erase copies already delivered.
If a shared cache reuses one user's personalized response for another, private content leaks; cookies and Set-Cookie do not automatically partition cache entries or universally prohibit caching.

Authorization-bearing requests have special shared-cache restrictions, but authentication is not a universal bypass guarantee under every response policy or CDN configuration. Keep origin authorization and verify explicit private/no-store policies plus CDN rules prevent shared storage and reuse of private-note responses.
criticalMisconceptions: no-cache means never store.
private forbids browser caching.
Cookie or authentication always creates a safe per-user CDN entry.
no-store replaces authorization or erases all existing copies.

questions.question: A public Notes export URL varies by ?format=pdf versus ?format=html and by Accept-Language: en versus fr. Define cache key, representation variant and Vary. Explain the required URL/query and header distinctions, what Vary: Accept-Language does, and what to verify if a CDN is configured to ignore query parameters. Explain both the danger of dropping a meaningful distinction and the hit-rate cost of keeping irrelevant tracking parameters; does Vary authorize sharing private notes?
criteria: A cache key identifies which stored response can satisfy a request; a representation variant is a different response form for the resource. HTTP caching uses method and target URL, with nominated request-header values distinguishing variants.
Keep format query values distinct because they change content; verify the CDN's actual key/query configuration rather than assuming every CDN includes every query parameter.
Vary: Accept-Language names the request header whose values must match for reuse, separating en and fr variants when the cache supports and honors that behavior; verify CDN support/configuration.

Dropping meaningful query or header distinctions can return the wrong format or language. Keeping irrelevant tracking parameters creates more entries and fewer hits; remove them only after establishing they do not affect the response.
Variant separation does not authorize public caching of private notes; privacy and authorization rules still apply.
criticalMisconceptions: Every CDN always includes all query parameters.
Vary changes the URL or overrides private/no-store.
Ignoring all query parameters is always safe.

questions.question: Notes deploys a changed app.js, edits a published page and unpublishes another page. Define a versioned asset URL and CDN purge. Explain a deployment using app.v2.js, what the page referencing it must do, how to manage freshness of a page that keeps the same URL, and why a database update or CDN purge does not instantly update every browser or revoke already delivered copies. State what to verify about purge coverage and completion.
criteria: A versioned URL changes when asset bytes change; publish app.v2.js and update the referring page to request it. Long caching is suitable when bytes at each versioned URL remain unchanged, but an old cached referring page can still request v1.
A mutable page retaining its URL needs a chosen freshness/revalidation policy consistent with tolerated delay; changing the database alone does not rewrite cached HTTP responses.
A CDN purge removes or invalidates targeted CDN entries according to the provider; verify the relevant URLs/variants, cache layers and completion/propagation behavior.

Purging CDN entries does not evict already fresh browser copies or erase delivered content. Unpublishing can stop future origin access and trigger purges but cannot promise instantaneous revocation of all cached/downloaded copies.
criticalMisconceptions: Changing database content immediately rewrites caches.
CDN purge clears every browser cache.
A versioned asset guarantees clients instantly obtain the page referencing it.
Unpublishing guarantees already delivered public content disappears.

questions.question: A public help page tolerates delay and has Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=30, stale-if-error=120. Assume the cache supports and permits these directives, has a stored eligible response, no conflicting directives and negligible transit time. Define both stale policies. At age 75 explain background revalidation; at age 150 with an eligible origin error explain fallback; at age 200 with the same error explain whether these directives still authorize stale reuse. Describe the availability limits if no copy exists, and why this policy may be unsuitable for private notes or urgent removal.
criteria: stale-while-revalidate permits serving a stale response for a bounded interval while attempting validation in the background; it hides validation latency rather than ensuring freshness.
Freshness lasts 60 seconds. At age 75, the response is 15 seconds stale and within the additional 30-second stale-while-revalidate window, which ends at age 90.

stale-if-error permits a stored stale response on eligible errors for an additional bounded interval after freshness expires. At age 150 the response is 90 seconds stale and within its 120-second window, which ends at age 180; at age 200 neither extension still authorizes reuse.

These permissions require cache support, applicable policy and an existing eligible response; a cold cache or expired allowance can still expose an origin failure. They do not guarantee availability or override storage/privacy restrictions.
Accepting stale public help content is a product decision; private-note correctness or urgent removal may require refusing stale reuse, and previously delivered copies still cannot be recalled.
criticalMisconceptions: Stale policies allow serving any old response forever.
stale-if-error manufactures a response on a cold miss.
A CDN guarantees origin outages are invisible.
Stale permissions override private/no-store.
